- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are flat or rising slowly, expect overshoot or overconfidence in early price spikes; adjust downward by 5–10% for the next 5–7 days.
- If supply net is negative and bearish sentiment dominates (≥0.50), model forecasts tend to underestimate downside risk; add 3–5% buffer to forecast lows.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overreacts and continues upward; cap forecast slope at 1–2% per day for 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.00–0.50), model tends to ignore event-driven volatility; increase forecast volatility by 10–20% for 3–7 days.
- If official events are frequent and supply net is negative, model underestimates downward pressure; shift forecast mean 2–5% lower for 5–10 days.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows mean reversion to 70–75 range after 10–15 days, model often fails to recognize it; apply mean reversion correction: target = 72–74 for 10–15 days.
- When sentiment is low and supply net is negative, model forecasts often lag by 2–3 days; adjust forecast to align with 1–2 days ahead of true outcome.
- If sentiment is bullish but true outcome shows sharp decline, model may misinterpret sentiment as signal; reduce forecast slope by 20–30% for 3–5 days.
